line: Good morning. Ernesto Villaseñor. I do the tax returns here on Saturdays, at the table by the kitchen. You are new in the neighbourhood?
choice1: Yes, I just moved in. I'm {playerName}.
choice2: Nice to meet you, Don Ernesto.
choice3: Sorry, I can't stop right now.

line: Welcome, then. If you worked at all last year, even a few months, you will probably need to file something. Do you have your W-2 yet, or is it still in an envelope?
choice3: I'll come back when I have it.

line: That is most people in February. Bring it unopened, I don't mind. One question, if you permit me: has anyone handed you a yellow flyer this week, with the word 'notario' on it?
choice1: I think so, at the bus stop. Why?
choice3: I'll bring the envelope by. Thanks.

line: Here I prepare taxes, that is all. In Guadalajara I was a notario for twenty-two years, which there is close to a lawyer, appointed by the state. Here a notary is a man with a stamp, and the flyers count on people not knowing that.
choice3: Good to know. I should go.

line: Immigration papers, mostly. They charge two thousand dollars for a form that is free, and some of them file nothing at all. Every spring somebody brings me a receipt, and all I can do is send them to the legal aid office on Fifth.
choice1: That must be hard to see.
choice3: I'll let you get back to it.

line: Some days, yes. I had an office on Avenida Juárez with my name on the door. At the hall I have a folding table next to the coffee urn, and on a Saturday in March the line still goes out the door.
choice1: Did you ever think about qualifying here?
choice3: I'll let you get back to it.

line: I thought about it. The exams, in English, at fifty-eight. I decided I would rather be very good at one form than a beginner at the law again. My son-in-law says that is pride. Maybe he is right.
choice1: Does it feel strange, starting over like that?
choice3: I should go. Good to meet you.

line: In Tepatitlán people still call me licenciado. At the hall the children call me Don Ernesto, and the bank writes Mr. Villasenor, without the tilde. I answer to all three. The third one took the longest.
choice2: Good to meet you, Don Ernesto.

line: If anyone you know has papers like that, bring them to the hall on a Saturday before they pay anyone. I read them for nothing. And keep your receipts, all of them, in one place. A shoebox is fine.
choice1: I'll come see you in February.

line: Ah, excuse me, I thought you were the young man from the desk. Ernesto Villaseñor. I do the tax returns at the parish hall on Grand, and I am looking for the drawer with the forms.
choice1: I'm {playerName}. I've been looking for it too.
choice2: Nice to meet you. Can I help?

line: It used to be in the cabinet by the copier. Now the cabinet has DVDs in it. Do you need a form yourself, or are you only being kind to an old man?
choice3: I hope you find it. I should go.

line: The 1040 is the easy part. The hard part is people who were told they cannot file because they have no Social Security number. They can, with an ITIN. I spend half of March explaining that.
choice2: How do you know all this?
choice3: Good to know. I'll let you look.

line: A tax number, for people the IRS knows about but Social Security does not. You file with it, you pay what you owe, and later the returns show you were here, working, all those years.
choice1: I'll tell my cousin about that.

line: Good morning, {playerName}. Sit, if you like. Nobody needs me for another half hour.
choice3: Just saying hello. See you later.

line: Good morning, {playerName}. Sit, if you like. Nobody needs me for another half hour.
choice3: Just saying hello. See you later.

line: Permit me a correction: the parish owns it, the bishop insures it, and {homeLead} runs it. Everybody else has opinions, myself included.

She is efficient, which I respect, and kind, which I respect more. She will talk to anyone: the alderman, the clinic, the man who fixes the boiler. $ My only footnote: she promises the library a little more than the hall can deliver. Then it delivers anyway, and I lose the argument.
Permit me a correction: the parish owns it. But on any question that matters, people ask {homeLead}. He has been in this building longer than the paint.

He is a man of his word, and his word is mostly 'ours.' One year I kept the Club's books. Very clean books. $ [guarded] He would not let me file the grant application. I still think he was wrong, and I still do his taxes.
Well, thank you. A little distracted. My granddaughter had her orchestra seating on Tuesday. Third chair, violin. I told her third is a fine chair, and she has not spoken to me since.
First, naturally. She practises in the kitchen an hour every night. Her mother says it is for the college applications. I think it is for her. Do you play anything?

Her teacher asked each of them to play something 'from home' for the winter concert. She chose Estrellita, by Manuel Ponce, and then she asked me who he was. I had to look it up. I did not tell her that.
choice3: I hope the concert goes well.

line: She was born here, on Dearborn Street, so she says here, and she is right. But she picked the Ponce, and nobody asked her to. I will be in the front row, and I will say nothing about third chair.
Ah, good morning. Have you seen the young man from the desk? The drawer with the tax forms has moved again.
choice1: I think it's by the copier.

line: By the copier was last year. I have explained to him twice where it should be. He is very polite about it, and then it moves.
choice1: Why do you need paper forms?
choice2: Maybe they move them on purpose.

line: Half my clients have no computer at home, and the ones who do don't want to put their name into a website. The paper they trust. And the paper comes with instructions in Spanish, if you ask at the desk.
choice1: Do they worry about filing at all?
choice2: Makes sense. I'll let you look.

line: Some do. The ones with an ITIN, especially, worry that a federal form with their address on it is a danger. I tell them what I know, that the return is proof they were here and paid. I do not tell them more than I know.
choice2: That's a lot to carry for people.
choice3: I should go. Good luck with the drawer.

line: Permit me to be careful. The law says the IRS keeps it private, and in eleven years nobody I filed for has had trouble from it. That is all I can say honestly. For more than that I send people to legal aid on Fifth.
Ah, {playerName}. Good, I hoped you would come by. Do you have five minutes? I have a question, and then a favour.
The question first. You ask me good questions, so I will ask you one. Honestly: do you keep your receipts?
choice3: Can we do this another time?

line: That can be fixed. Now the favour. In March I have more people than hours, and I need someone at the door with the list, telling people which papers to bring next time. In Spanish and in English.
It doesn't need to be great. Half my clients speak English when their children are with them and switch to Spanish when the numbers get serious. You will keep up.
Good. Saturdays in March, nine to one. You will hear a great deal about people's lives at that door. You keep all of it to yourself. That is the only rule I have.
choice1: I can do that. See you in March.

line: Good afternoon. Excuse the folders, I am taking some files over to the parish office.
To the cabinet with the lock. Three clients asked me this week to take their returns out of my files completely, after the speech. As if paper could make them invisible.
choice3: That's hard. I'll let you go.

line: I told them that filing is the proof they were here, working, paying. If they stop now, they lose the years they already have. Two of them understood. The third took his folder home.
choice2: I might have done the same.

line: I don't know, and I will not guess to his face. I told him my table is at the hall again in February. That is what I can offer him that is true.
Good afternoon. Excuse me one moment, I am reading the new rule from the clinic. Twice, to be sure.
The clinic can now help people apply for benefits directly. That is good. It also means that in April I will have twice the people at my table asking which line is line 11.
choice3: I'll let you get back to it.

line: Maybe. I wouldn't mind. For years people brought me things that were not taxes at all, the school letters, the gas company, because I was the one who reads forms.
A little, yes. In Guadalajara people also came to me with everything in one folder, the deed and the birth certificate and the letter from the cousin. I am used to being the man with the folder.
Ah, {playerName}. {homeLead} tells me you are at the hall nearly every day now.
Not at all. The hall needs young people who can lift tables. Also ones who can read a W-2, but I don't hope for miracles.
When I first came, I stayed away from the hall for almost a year. I did not want to be only the man from Jalisco who used to be somebody. Then I found nobody there thought of me that way except me.
A lady at the pantry asked me to look at her late husband's pension letter. I came the next Saturday with a folding table, in case anyone else had a letter. That was eleven years ago.
Good afternoon. I have not seen you at the hall for a while.
choice1: I've been at the library a lot.

line: {homeLead} said the library. It's a good library. Very complete. Except the drawer with the forms, which I have now found, so you can stop looking.
Tuesdays, for the newspapers. The local one, the one from Guadalajara on their computer, and the Spanish one from the city. By the third one I usually know what actually happened.

Each one about different things. But none of them writes about the people in my line on a Saturday. For that you have to sit at my table at the hall. That is my whole sales pitch, and I will not make it twice.
Don Ernesto inclines his head, very correctly, and goes back to his papers.
choice1: Don Ernesto, I owe you an apology.

line: Accepted. It was not a large offence. Next time you are in a hurry, just tell me you are in a hurry. I understand hurry.
One moment, please. I am adding a column, and if I lose the column I lose the morning.
